1.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and controls e4 and d5 without committing a pawn, so Black keeps every set-up open and sees White's plan first. It also makes 2.e4 pointless, since the pawn is simply lost to ...Nxe4. The cost is that Black must be at home in several different structures.

1.Nf3 d5.strategy: Claims the centre at once and turns 2.e4 into a gambit, since ...dxe4 takes the pawn. Black gets an early stake in the middle, but White keeps the choice between quiet set-ups that leave the d5-pawn alone and a direct challenge to it, and Black must be ready for both.

1.Nf3 c5.strategy: Fights for d4 at once: if White takes the centre with a pawn, Black trades a flank pawn for a centre pawn. It suits a player who already answers 1.e4 with 1...c5, but White decides whether the game becomes a Sicilian or a symmetrical English, so Black must be ready for either.

1.Nf3 e6.strategy: Opens the f8-bishop and prepares ...d5 while keeping the king's knight and the c-pawn uncommitted. Black can still choose between several solid set-ups. The cost is that White picks the type of game, and after ...d5 the c8-bishop stays hemmed in behind the e6-pawn.

1.Nf3 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7 and leaves the centre for later. The fianchettoed bishop presses on White's centre from a distance, and Black counterattacks with pawn breaks in the centre or on the queenside. White can gain space with pawns on e4 and d4, so Black must be ready to hit the centre.

1.Nf3 f5.strategy: Takes control of e4 and aims for set-ups in which Black fights for the centre from the flank. Sound and established, but sharper and more committal than the quieter main replies, because it weakens the e8–h5 diagonal and the e6-square. White can test it at once with the gambit 2.e4 fxe4 3.Ng5, which attacks the e4-pawn.

1.Nf3 c6.name: Zukertort Opening: Slav Invitation
1.Nf3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with the pawn supported, aiming at solid Slav or Caro-Kann structures. It is sound but more passive than the main replies, because the c-pawn move does not develop a piece.

1.Nf3 d6.name: Zukertort Opening: Pirc Invitation
1.Nf3 d6.strategy: Keeps the centre flexible and waits for White to commit. Sound, but it gives White a free hand to build a broad pawn centre, while the d6-pawn only watches e5 and c5.

1.Nf3 b6.name: Zukertort Opening: Queenside Fianchetto Variation
1.Nf3 b6.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto ...Bb7, which presses on e4 along the long diagonal. The set-up is sound but slow: White can take the centre at once, and Black has to attack the pawns afterwards.

1.Nf3 Nc6.name: Zukertort Opening: Black Mustang Defence
1.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a knight and watches e5 and d4, so Black keeps its central pawn breaks open. The knight blocks the c-pawn and commits itself before White shows a plan. Sound enough, but Black gains nothing over the main replies.

1.Nf3 a6.name: Zukertort Opening: St. George Defence
1.Nf3 a6.background: 1...a6 is the move of the St. George Defence against 1.e4, on which the English IM Michael Basman did much of the theoretical work and with which Tony Miles beat the reigning world champion Anatoly Karpov at the 1980 European Team Championship in Skara.
1.Nf3 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5 and ...Bb7, but spends a tempo on a rim pawn while White takes the centre. Nothing in the position makes the move urgent, so Black falls behind in space and development.

1.Nf3 a5.name: Zukertort Opening: Ware Defence
1.Nf3 a5.strategy: Gains a little space on the queenside but does nothing for the centre or development, and leaves b6 without the a-pawn's protection. White builds a centre and keeps the extra tempo.

1.Nf3 b5.name: Zukertort Opening: Polish Defence
1.Nf3 b5.strategy: Claims queenside space and prepares ...Bb7, but the pawn on b5 needs constant protection and the c6-square is weakened. White gains time against it with e4, which opens the f1-bishop's diagonal to b5, or with a4.

1.Nf3 Na6.strategy: Heads for b4 or c5, but the knight on the rim covers no central square and blocks the a-pawn. White takes space in the centre and keeps the initiative.

1.Nf3 Nh6.strategy: Eyes f5, but the knight on the rim covers no central square, and after 2.d4 the c1-bishop can take it, doubling Black's h-pawns. Black loses time and White gets the centre without a fight.

1.Nf3 f6.name: Zukertort Opening: Arctic Defence
1.Nf3 f6.strategy: Prepares ...e5, but takes the g8-knight's best square and loosens e6 and the e8–h5 diagonal. After 2.e4 e5 3.Nxe5, taking the knight with 3...fxe5? runs into 4.Qh5+ and a decisive attack.

1.Nf3 h6.name: Zukertort Opening: Basman Defence
1.Nf3 h6.strategy: Prepares ...g5 and ...g4 against the knight on f3, but loses a tempo and loosens the kingside. White builds a centre while Black's flank play achieves little.

1.Nf3 h5.strategy: Spends a tempo on a flank pawn and gives up control of g5, where White's knight can settle because ...h6 is no longer possible. It does nothing for the centre or development.

1.Nf3 e5.name: Zukertort Opening: Ross Gambit
1.Nf3 e5.strategy: Walks into 2.Nxe5, which wins the unprotected pawn. After 2...Nc6 3.Nxc6 dxc6 Black has open lines and quick development, but not enough for the pawn.

1.Nf3 g5.name: Zukertort Opening: Herrstrom Gambit
1.Nf3 g5.strategy: Offers the g-pawn for nothing: 2.Nxg5 wins it, and 2...e5, which uncovers the queen's attack on the knight, only drives it back while White keeps the extra pawn and Black's kingside stays weakened.

1.Nf3.name: Zukertort Opening
1.Nf3.background: Named after Johannes Zukertort. Most sources call only 1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 the Réti Opening, the line with which Richard Réti beat the reigning world champion Capablanca at New York 1924. Réti championed the hypermodern school of the 1920s, which controlled the centre from a distance rather than occupying it with pawns.
